teaser: The most parodied couple in America is not a couple, and never stood in front of that house.

lesson.text: You have met these two before, even if you have never seen the painting. They have been redrawn as presidents, cartoon families, puppets, pets and zombies. They have sold cereal and insurance. Stand two people side by side, hand one a tool, keep a straight face, and everyone gets the reference.

The original is smaller than its fame: about 78 by 65 centimeters (31 by 26 inches), painted in 1930 on beaverboard, a cheap panel of pressed wood fiber. Its painter, Grant Wood, was a 39-year-old from Cedar Rapids, Iowa, almost unknown outside his state.

It began with a house, not with people. In the small town of Eldon, Iowa, Wood noticed a plain white cottage with one fancy church-style window upstairs. He sketched it on the spot and decided to paint the kind of people he imagined should live there.

That pointed window explains the title. “Carpenter Gothic” was the name for wooden American houses that borrowed shapes from medieval Gothic cathedrals. Wood found the ambition both funny and touching. Then he built his whole picture out of the window's tall, upright lines.
Four shapes that rhyme with each other.

lines.label: The window
lines.text: A pointed arch split by a thin center bar: the Gothic detail that started everything.

lines.label: The pitchfork
lines.text: Three prongs, close to dead center, gripped like a weapon. It stands between you and the house like a gate.

lines.label: The overalls
lines.text: The seams on the bib repeat the fork: three uprights joined by a curve. Wood hid the tool in the man's own clothes.

lines.label: The faces
lines.text: Even the heads obey. Both faces are pulled long and narrow, like the boards on the wall behind them.

lesson.text: Window, fork, seams, faces: everything stands at attention. The stiffness was a choice. On a trip to Munich in 1928 Wood had studied Flemish and German portraits of the 1400s, with their hard outlines, glassy detail and unsmiling sitters, and he decided to paint Iowa the same way.

The pair never stood in front of the house, or even together. The woman is Wood's sister, Nan Wood Graham, then about 30. The man is his dentist, Dr. Byron McKeeby, 62. Each posed separately. And they are not meant as husband and wife: Wood described them as a farmer and his grown daughter.

Wood dressed Nan in an old-fashioned apron and pulled her hair back tight, the way women appear in family photographs from the 1800s. Everything about her is buttoned, pinned and ironed. Almost everything.
One thing about the woman has escaped her tidy control. Tap it.

spots.title: The loose curl
spots.text: A single strand of hair has slipped free and snakes down behind her ear. It is the one disorderly thing in the entire picture, and it makes her human.

lesson.text: That curl hangs beside the other telling detail: the eyes. He stares straight at you through round glasses, guarding the doorstep. She looks off to the side, at something we cannot see. Two people a foot apart, in different worlds. Is she anxious, bored, disapproving? Wood leaves it hanging.

Wood entered the painting in a competition at the Art Institute of Chicago in the fall of 1930. It won a bronze medal and a $300 prize, and the museum bought it for another $300. It has stayed there ever since.

Then newspapers printed it, and Iowa was not amused. Readers wrote in, furious that Wood had painted them as grim, pinched fanatics. He protested that he was an Iowan himself and meant affection, not mockery. He never fully settled the matter, and the picture works either way.

The mood flipped within a few years. As the Great Depression deepened, the same hard faces began to look like stubborn people who would get through it. A satire became a patriotic emblem, and Wood became the star of Regionalism, a group of painters who turned away from European abstraction toward scenes of the rural Midwest.
A picture that reads as mockery and as praise has to be built with great care. Wood filled it with small, exact things, each one a clue about this household. Wander around and collect them.

spots.title: The cameo
spots.text: A carved brooch with a woman's profile, the single ornament she allows herself. Wood is said to have bought it in Italy as a present for his mother.

spots.title: Porch plants
spots.text: Potted plants on the porch, among them a spiky snake plant. Somebody waters these. It is the gentlest corner of the picture, and it is on her side.

spots.title: The drawn curtain
spots.text: The Gothic window is covered by a patterned curtain in broad daylight. Whatever goes on in this house is private.

spots.title: Round glasses
spots.text: Thin wire spectacles and a mouth set like a ruled line. The model was a dentist, not a farmer: this expression is what Wood asked for, not a portrait of the man's character.

spots.title: The red barn
spots.text: A barn slips in at the right edge, the strongest warm color in the picture. That side is his territory, as the porch plants are hers.

spots.title: The apron
spots.text: A brown print apron dotted with tiny circles and edged with rickrack, a zigzag trim. It was already old-fashioned in 1930.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: GRANT WOOD 1930, lettered on the denim at the bottom edge, as if stitched into the overalls.

lesson.text: The house still stands in Eldon, Iowa. A visitor center next door lends out aprons, jackets and a pitchfork so that people can pose for the photograph themselves.
American Gothic rests on one repeated upright shape and one unanswered question: is Wood laughing at these people or honoring them? Because it never answers, it can be reused for anything.

Not every remake is a joke. In 1942 the photographer Gordon Parks posed Ella Watson, a Black cleaning woman in a government building in Washington, in front of the American flag, a broom in one hand and a mop behind her. He called the photograph American Gothic. Same stiff pose, a very different America.

quiz.question: What inspired Grant Wood to make the painting?
options: A small house with a Gothic-style window
quiz.explanation: He saw the cottage in Eldon, Iowa, and imagined who should live in it.

quiz.question: Who posed for the two figures?
options: A farmer and his wife from Eldon
quiz.explanation: Nan Wood Graham and Dr. Byron McKeeby posed separately.

quiz.question: Which shape does Wood repeat across the picture?
options: The three prongs of the pitchfork
quiz.explanation: The fork returns in the seams of the overalls and echoes the window and the long faces.

quiz.question: How did many Iowans react at first?
options: They were angry at being shown as grim
quiz.explanation: Readers wrote to newspapers, furious at the portrayal.

quiz.question: What is beaverboard?
options: A cheap panel of pressed wood fiber
quiz.explanation: Wood painted on this inexpensive building material.

quiz.question: Where does the woman look?
quiz.explanation: The man stares at us while she looks away at something outside the picture.

facts.text: According to Wood, the two figures are a farmer and his daughter.
facts.explanation: He described them that way, not as husband and wife.

facts.text: The two models posed together in front of the house in Eldon.
facts.explanation: They posed separately and never stood in front of the house.

facts.text: Gordon Parks borrowed the title American Gothic for a 1942 photograph.
facts.explanation: His portrait of Ella Watson with broom and mop uses the same pose and name.
